questions.question: What does a number actually represent?
options: A quantity, amount, or position in a sequence
A type of letter used only in mathematics
A drawing of the object being counted
A word that means the same thing in every language
questions.rationale: A number is a symbol that stands in for "how many" or "how much" — that's why 5 apples and 5 chairs can share the exact same number, even though the objects are completely different.

questions.question: You count 7 goats by pointing at each one and saying one count-word per goat, never skipping or repeating an animal. What is this method called?
questions.rationale: Matching exactly one count-word to exactly one object is one-to-one correspondence — the oldest and most basic way humans have ever counted, long before written number symbols existed.

questions.question: On a number line, what does the point marked 0 represent?
options: The starting point that every other number is measured from
The largest number on the line
questions.rationale: 0 isn't "nothing happened" — it's the fixed starting point. Every other position on the line is described by how far it is from that starting point.

questions.question: Which set of numbers includes 0, but does NOT include negative numbers?
questions.rationale: Whole numbers are natural numbers plus 0 (0, 1, 2, 3, …) — still no negatives. Negatives only enter with integers.

questions.question: Which family of numbers was invented specifically to answer "what if we go below zero?"
questions.rationale: Integers extend whole numbers downward past zero: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … — the first number family that can represent "less than nothing."

questions.question: 3/4 belongs to which family of numbers?
questions.rationale: A rational number can be written as one whole number divided by another (a fraction). 3/4 is exactly that, so it's rational — not a natural or whole number, since those can't represent parts of a whole.

questions.question: Which of these numbers is irrational?
questions.rationale: √2 goes on forever without ever repeating a pattern, so it can't be written as a simple fraction — that makes it irrational. 1/2, 0.75, and 5 can all be written as exact fractions, so they're rational.

questions.question: True or false: every whole number is also a rational number.
options: True — each number family sits inside the next one
False — whole numbers and rational numbers never overlap
True, but only for whole numbers greater than 10
False — only integers can be rational
questions.rationale: Nothing gets thrown away moving from one family to the next. Natural numbers sit inside whole numbers, which sit inside integers, which sit inside rational numbers — every whole number 7 is also the rational number 7/1.

questions.question: In the number 352, what is the value of the digit 5?
questions.rationale: 352 = 3×100 + 5×10 + 2×1. The 5 sits in the tens place, so it's worth 5 × 10 = 50 — not just "five," because of where it sits.

questions.question: Why are 352 and 325 different numbers, even though they use the exact same three digits?
options: They aren't actually different — it's just a writing style choice
Because place value gives each digit a different worth depending on its position
Because 325 uses a secret extra digit
Because one of them is irrational
questions.rationale: Place value means position changes worth. In 352 the 3 is worth 300; in 325 the 3 is worth only 3. Same digits, different positions, different numbers.
